analysis.one_liner: Requires upwind areas to cut ozone smog pollution or pay downwind areas' cleanup costs.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan clean-air bill with 12 cosponsors from both parties that would have made upwind areas cut smog-forming pollution or pay for downwind cleanup died in a House subcommittee without ever getting a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Clean Air Act so that any area or state whose pollution significantly contributes to smog (ozone) violations somewhere else would have to either cut its own emissions in proportion to its contribution, or pay the downwind area's cleanup costs. It also would have required stricter vehicle smog-check programs in moderate pollution areas that send pollution downwind, and barred upwind areas from weakening existing controls while they still contributed to another area's smog problem.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live downwind of major pollution sources — residents of ozone nonattainment areas that receive pollution blown in from elsewhere. Ozone (smog) aggravates asthma and other respiratory disease, so downwind residents would get cleaner air either through actual emission cuts in the upwind area or through upwind-funded cleanup measures locally. Air quality districts in downwind areas would also gain a funding stream if upwind areas chose the payment option. The bill's sponsors were largely from California, where the Central Valley and other regions receive transported pollution.

how_it_helps.text: Requires upwind areas to reduce ozone-forming emissions by an amount matching their contribution to downwind pollution, or instead make payments covering the cost of fully mitigating the pollution they send downwind.

Requires enhanced vehicle inspection and maintenance (stricter smog-check) programs in moderate ozone nonattainment areas that significantly contribute to downwind violations — vehicle exhaust is a major source of the pollutants that form ozone.

Locks in existing controls: an upwind area that had been reclassified as meeting air standards would have to keep implementing every control measure from its old plan, with no relaxation or rescission, as long as it still contributed to smog violations downwind.

For pollution crossing state lines, the Environmental Protection Agency (not the polluting state) would determine whether the upwind state causes or significantly contributes to a downwind violation, closing off the option of an upwind state simply denying responsibility.

analysis.who_pays: Upwind areas and states: the power plants, factories, and other sources there would bear the cost of emission reductions, or the cost of compensation payments to downwind areas. Motorists in upwind moderate nonattainment areas would face stricter and more expensive vehicle inspection programs. Upwind areas that had won reclassification as clean would lose the ability to drop their old control measures.
analysis.who_pays_short: Upwind industries, power plants, and motorists

drawbacks.text: The bill lets upwind areas pay money instead of cutting their own emissions (Sec. 2(a)(B)), which compensates the downwind area's cleanup but does not by itself reduce the pollution actually drifting downwind — a polluter could buy its way out of cleaning up.

For pollution within a state, the bill lets the state itself determine whether its upwind area is causing a downwind violation (Sec. 2(a)(4)), so states could be tempted to never make that determination for their own areas; only interstate pollution is policed by the EPA.
Enhanced vehicle inspection and maintenance programs cost motorists in upwind moderate areas real money in test and repair expenses, which falls hardest on lower-income drivers with older cars.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — cleaner air for people breathing pollution produced somewhere else — was real and the bill addressed a genuine gap in the Clean Air Act, since downwind areas are otherwise stuck with pollution they cannot control. But the design had holes an honest supporter would concede: the pay-instead-of-clean option lets pollution continue as long as checks are written, and the state-self-determination provision for in-state areas invited evasion. The costs to upwind industry and to upwind motorists were real but modest compared with the health stakes for downwind populations.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Commerce Committee and then to its Health and Environment subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing, a markup, or a vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Gary Condit of California introduced the bill on July 31, 1997, with 11 cosponsors from both parties, most of them from California downwind districts.
It was referred to the House Committee on Commerce the same day.
On August 18, 1997, it was sent to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment — the last action ever taken on the bill.
The subcommittee and full committee never reported the bill, and it never reached the House floor before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Upwind power plants, industrial sources, and motorists were better off because the bill died — they avoided new emission-reduction duties, compensation payments, and stricter smog checks. Downwind residents got no relief from the pollution they receive from upwind areas.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Upwind industries avoided new cleanup costs

for.name: Rep. Gary Condit
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill; represented a California district affected by transported air pollution

for.name: 12 House cosponsors (8 Democrats, 4 Republicans)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors, giving the bill bipartisan sponsorship from districts including California, Texas, Alabama, Virginia, and Minnesota

against.name: House Committee on Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral, passed it to its Health and Environment subcommittee, and never reported it out; no hearing or markup is recorded

against.name: Subcommittee on Health and Environment
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after the August 18, 1997 referral for the remaining 16 months of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes, so no partisan split is recorded; sponsorship itself was bipartisan, with 8 Democratic and 4 Republican cosponsors joining the Democratic sponsor.

industries.industry: Upwind power plants and industrial emitters
industries.note: Interstate ozone transport comes overwhelmingly from large stationary sources like power plant and factory stacks. The bill would have required their states to cut emissions commensurate with their contribution to downwind smog, or pay the downwind area's mitigation costs, so these sources would have borne the direct expense.

industries.industry: Motor vehicle owners in upwind areas
industries.note: Motorists in upwind moderate nonattainment areas would have faced enhanced inspection and maintenance programs — more frequent and stricter smog tests and any repairs needed to pass. That is a real household cost, though it targets vehicle exhaust, a leading source of ozone-forming pollution.

Enhanced smog-check mandates create mandatory testing and repair work. Their gain is tied to a mandate that also serves the public health purpose, though the bill's failure means none of this materialized.
If upwind areas chose the payment option, districts in downwind areas would receive compensation funding earmarked for local emission-reduction measures.
